Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Host–Virus Immune Interactions in Andes Virus Infection: Implications for Human-to-Human Transmission, Pathogenesis, and Public Health
papers.abstract: The Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus, andesense) is unique among hantaviruses in that it may transfer from person to person and cause severe vascular damage. The evidence on host–virus immunological interactions and their importance in disease progression, transmission, and public health is compiled in this narrative review. ANDV mostly affects pulmonary endothelial cells and does not result in widespread cell loss. Rather, the loss of vascular barrier integrity is caused by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) activation, breakdown of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin, hypoxia-related pathways, and mediators produced from infected pericytes. Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)–interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns

source_records.title: Host–Virus Immune Interactions in Andes Virus Infection: Implications for Human-to-Human Transmission, Pathogenesis, and Public Health
source_records.abstract: The Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus, andesense) is unique among hantaviruses in that it may transfer from person to person and cause severe vascular damage. The evidence on host–virus immunological interactions and their importance in disease progression, transmission, and public health is compiled in this narrative review. ANDV mostly affects pulmonary endothelial cells and does not result in widespread cell loss. Rather, the loss of vascular barrier integrity is caused by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) activation, breakdown of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin, hypoxia-related pathways, and mediators produced from infected pericytes. Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)–interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns

papers.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis
papers.abstract: Abstract Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli -based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.

Genomics & Informatics (2026) 24:19 1 Introduction Nephropathia epidemica (NE) is attributed to Puumala virus (PUUV), a naturally occurring form of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in humans, which is a zoonotic infectious disease and generally considered a mild-to-moderate form of hantavirus infection within the HFRS spectrum [1–4]. PUUV (Puumala orthohantavi- rus) is classified within the genus Orthohantavirus, fam- ily Hantaviridae, and order Bunyavirales, as defined by current ICTV taxonomy, and it was previously grouped under the family Bunyaviridae prior to taxonomic reclas- sification [5, 6]. PUUV infection presents with highly variable out- comes, ranging from subclinical cases (70–80%) to severe HFRS, and carries a fatality rate of about 0.1% [7]. PUUV infection commonly presents with sudden fever, head- ache, back pain, nausea, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, hematuria, and varying degrees of acute kidney impairment [1, 8]. In some patients, addi- tional manifestations such as blurred vision, dizziness, insomnia, respiratory complications, oliguria, and sub- sequent polyuria during recovery may also occur [2, 9]. Although PUUV infection is generally considered mild, severe complications can occur in a subset of patients, including acute kidney failure, hypotension, shock, pul- monary edema, Guillain-Barré syndrome, respiratory distress, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), myocarditis, encephalitis, pituitary hemorrhage, seizures, and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure or fatal cerebral hemorrhage [2, 3, 10, 11]. The first identification of PUUV occurred in the early 1980s when the virus was isolated from bank voles (Myodes glareolus) in the Puumala region of Finland [2]. Between July 1989 and June 1996, Finland reported 6701 PUUV infection cases confirmed via serologi- cal assays, with the highest incidence in the Itä-Savo district and a mortality rate below 0.1%, and later from 1995 to 2008, 22,681 cases were recorded with an average annual incidence of 31 per 100,000 population, resulting in 13 deaths and 52% of patients requiring hospitaliza- tion [12, 13]. PUUV accounts for approximately 93% of all notified hantavirus infections in Germany and caused a major outbreak in 2007 in Baden-Württemberg with 1089 reported human cases, while the highest annual number of PUUV infections in Germany was recorded in 2010 since hantavirus surveillance began in 2001 [14, 15]. Also in 2007, Sweden’s Västerbotten County experi- enced a surprisingly severe outbreak of PUUV infection, with NE rates hitting 313 cases per 100,000 residents [16, 17]. Between 2001 and 2017, a total of 12,148 hantavirus disease cases were recorded, of which 9714 (approxi- mately 97.41%) were attributed to PUUV infection [18]. In 2019, Europe recorded over 4000 hantavirus cases (0.8 per 100,000), 98% caused by PUUV, with Finland and Germany making up 69% of the total [19]. From 2018 to 2025, Hungary recorded 51 lab-confirmed hantavirus infections, 20 of which were specifically linked to the PUUV [20]. In Finland, between 560 and 3800 cases of NE are reported each year, though the actual number is believed to be nearly six times higher [21]. PUUV is a spherical enveloped pathogen character- ized by a segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome [5, 21]. The PUUV possesses a tripartite genome: the L segment (~ 6.5 kb) encodes a ~ 2156-amino-acid L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) with replicase, transcriptase, and endo- nuclease functions; the M segment (~ 3.7 kb) encodes a ~ 1148-amino-acid glycoprotein precursor that is co- translationally cleaved into Gn (70 kDa) and Gc (55 kDa); and the S segment (~ 1.8 kb) encodes a ~ 433-amino-acid nucleocapsid (N) protein [2, 5, 22, 23]. Gc is the protein that mediates fusion by the identification of a peptide of fusion, whereas Gn serves as a folding chaperone for Gc and controls the time of fusion; both are necessary for the virus to adhere as well as enter host cells [2, 24]. Gn and Gc form the principal antigenic surface of PUUV and are major targets of neutralizing antibodies, contributing to protective immunity and vaccine relevance [25–27]. The N protein plays multiple roles in viral genome transport, replication, and assembly through its interactions with host cellular proteins, while also acting as a highly immu- nogenic viral component in both humans and animal models [28, 29]. The N protein is highly conserved among orthohantaviruses and elicits a strong early antibody response during acute infection, making it an important target for both diagnostic applications and vaccine devel- opment [30, 31]. Various vaccine platforms are available, each possess- ing distinct advantages and drawbacks. For example, live attenuated vaccines trigger strong, long-lasting immu- nity but can be risky for immunocompromised individu- als due to possible reversion to virulence; inactivated vaccines are safer and more stable, though they usually require multiple doses; subunit vaccines use only key antigens, lowering the chance of side effects, but often need adjuvants and booster shots to achieve durable pro- tection [32–35]. Moreover, DNA vaccines offer rapid, stable, and cost-effective production with long-lasting immunity, but they often show weak immunogenicity in humans and face delivery challenges [34, 36]. In con- trast, the key advantage of mRNA vaccines lies in their rapid design and production, enabling swift responses to emerging infections and pandemic threats without the need to culture live pathogens [37, 38]. In recognition of these advances, the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman Page 3 of 26 Hossain et al. Genomics & Informatics (2026) 24:19 for their groundbreaking contributions to nucleoside engineering, a key innovation that enabled the successful development of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 [39]. Recent developments in bioinformatics have improved biopharmaceutical design by enabling rapid prediction of protein features, structural modeling, and immuno- genicity assessment. These computational approaches accelerate the identification and optimization of thera- peutic candidates while reducing time and experimental costs; however, challenges related to prediction accuracy, biological complexity, and the need for experimental validation remain important considerations [40]. Reverse vaccinology (RV) applies bioinformatics and immuno- informatics to screen microbial genomes for conserved, immunogenic epitopes, enabling faster, safer, and cost- effective vaccine development compared to traditional pathogen culturing, a slow and labor-intensive process [41, 42]. Vaccine development against PUUV infection has included inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recom- binant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccines [43–45]. Among these, inactivated and DNA vaccine candidates have demon- strated promising immunogenicity in preclinical studies [44–46]. Currently, no vaccine has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for PUUV infection [9, 47]. Several studies have suggested the potential of multi- epitope vaccine approaches using immunoinformatics- based strategies. Khan et al. developed a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against SARS-CoV-2 by integrating epitope prediction, antigenicity assessment, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response analysis, demonstrating the feasibility of com- putational vaccine design approaches [48]. Similarly, Peele et al. designed a multi-epitope vaccine construct containing predicted B-cell and T-cell epitopes and evaluated its structural and immunological proper- ties through computational analyses [49]. These studies highlighted the potential of combining multiple immune targets within a single vaccine construct; however, their findings remained primarily dependent on computa- tional predictions and required experimental validation to confirm immunogenicity and protective efficacy. However, despite these advances, several challenges remain in current multi-epitope vaccine development strategies. Computational vaccine designs are depend- ent on prediction algorithms, reference databases, structural modeling assumptions, and available biologi- cal information, which may influence the reliability of predicted vaccine candidates. In addition, variations in epitope selection criteria, antigen conservation analysis, population coverage evaluation, and structural validation approaches can affect the effectiveness of computational vaccine design. Recent studies have emphasized that although immunoinformatics approaches accelerate multi-epitope vaccine development, comprehensive experimental validation remains essential for confirming biological relevance and protective potential [50]. Despite previous vaccine development efforts, includ- ing inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subu- nit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccine candidates, no PUUV vaccine has currently received regulatory approval. An integrated mRNA multi-epitope vaccine strategy targeting con- served regions of both PUUV glycoproteins (Gn/Gc) and nucleocapsid protein remains insufficiently explored. A comprehensive framework combining conserved antigen identification, multi-epitope vaccine construction, struc- tural evaluation, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction for PUUV has not been extensively investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to design and evaluate the PV-GNProtecta vaccine candidate using an integrated immunoinfor- matics workflow involving conserved antigen identifica- tion, epitope prediction, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction. The findings provide computational insights into the potential characteristics of PV-GNPro- tecta while recognizing the necessity of experimental val- idation for future assessment. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Acquisition and characterization of viral protein sequences The UniProt protein database (https://​www.​unipr​ot.​org/; accessed on 15 July 2025) was used for obtaining amino acid sequences of the target proteins from PUUV of G (accession number: P41266) and N (accession numbers: P41270) [51]. The G and N proteins were selected due to their key roles in PUUV infection and immune recogni- tion. The G protein mediates viral attachment and entry and is a major target of neutralizing antibodies, whereas the highly conserved N protein contributes to viral repli- cation and induces strong immune responses. Compared with the intracellular RdRp/L protein, G and N provide more suitable targets for antibody and cellular immune responses. A comparative evaluation of these proteins is provided in Supplementary Table S14. 2.2 Physicochemical and structural characterization of selected proteins The selected PUUV G and N proteins were character- ized for signal peptide presence, transmembrane regions, and subcellular localization. Signal peptide predic- tion was performed using SignalP 6.0 (https://​servi​ces.​ healt​htech.​dtu.​dk/​servi​ces/​Signa​lP-6.​0/; accessed on 15 Page 4 of 26 Hossain et al. Genomics & Informatics (2026) 24:19 September 2026) with the organism group selected as Eukarya and the default prediction model [52]. Trans- membrane topology was predicted using DeepTMHMM version 1.0.57 (accessed on 15 September 2026) using the default settings [53]. Subcellular localization informa- tion was obtained from UniProt (https://​www.​unipr​ot.​ org/; accessed on 15 September 2026) based on available curated annotations [54]. 2.3 Analysis of multiple sequence alignment and evolutionary relationships To support RV analysis, the sequence is encoded using amino acid residue codes and preserved as a FASTA sequence file. The acquired sequences were subsequently utilized for multiple sequence alignment (MSA) through the Clustal Omega platform (https://​www.​ebi.​ac.​uk/​ jdisp​atcher/​msa/​clust​alo; accessed on 05 August 2025) [55]. The Mega X tool (https://​www.​megas​oftwa​re.​net/; accessed on 05 August 2025) was employed for phyloge- netic analysis on both genomes [56]. 2.4 Prediction of epitopes for MHC I, MHC II, and linear B‐cell interactions The MHC I epitopes from the G and N proteins were found using the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) (http://​tools.​iedb.​org/​mhci/; accessed on 20 August 2025) software, with a percentile rank < 1.00 as the selec- tion criterion [57]. This tool is a sophisticated database comprising information on MHC molecules, T-cell and B-cell epitopes, antibodies, and MHC-binding ligands identified in humans and various animal taxonomic groups, including primates and rodents [58, 59]. A cut- off percentile rank of less than 1.00 was implemented for epitope selection, which suggests that the binding affinity was improved [37]. Lower percentile rank values indicate stronger predicted peptide–MHC binding affin- ity [60]. The IEDB (http://​tools.​iedb.​org/​mhcii/; accessed on 20 August 2025) was applied to forecast the MHC II epitopes inside the designated areas of these proteins, and peptides with percentile ranks < 1.00 were considered potential high-affinity binders and selected for further evaluation [61]. Subsequently, the human allele reference sets were employed to predict CD8 + and CD4 + bind- ing. The ABCpred tool (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​ va/​abcpr​ed/; accessed on 25 August 2025) was used to estimate the continuous B-cell epitopes of the selected portions of these proteins. This tool provides epitope predictions by analyzing the sequence features of the tar- get antigens [58, 62]. This program uses an affinity scale method based on a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to predict continuous B-cell epitopes [63, 64]. Additionally, the MHC-II epitopes underwent some additional analy- ses, including IL-10 (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​ il10p​red/; accessed on 25 September 2026), IFN-gamma (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​ifnep​itope/​predi​ct.​ php; accessed on 25 September 2026), IL-2 (https://​webs.​ iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​il2pr​ed/; accessed on 25 September 2026) and IL-4 (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​il4pr​ ed/​design.​php; accessed on 25 September 2026) by using the respective servers. Genomics & Informatics Design and in silico evaluation of PV‐GNProtecta: an mRNA multi‐epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis Tanvir Hossain1, Abdullah Al Mahmud1, Maisha Afrin2, Sakibur Rahman1, Shaheda Siddiqa Tahia1, Ahmad Abdullah Mahdeen3* and Md. Habib Ullah Masum4* Abstract Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population cov- erage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escheri- chia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection. analysis.background: PUUV is the principal cause of nephropathia epidemica, a zoonotic disease with renal complications and no approved vaccine, representing a public‑health threat.
analysis.methods: An immunoinformatics pipeline used conserved glycoprotein G and nucleoprotein N regions to design the mRNA multi‑epitope vaccine PV‑GNProtecta, including epitope prediction, population‑coverage analysis, physicochemical assessment, structural modeling, TLR4 docking, MM‑GBSA, 100 ns molecular dynamics, codon optimization for E. coli, and immune‑simulation.
analysis.results: The selected T‑ and B‑cell epitopes were highly antigenic, non‑allergenic and non‑toxic; population coverage was broad across diverse HLA alleles; the construct showed favorable stability, solubility and antigenicity; 95.5 % of residues fell in favored Ramachandran regions with an ERRAT score of 91.4; docking and MM‑GBSA indicated strong binding to TLR4 and MD showed a stable complex; codon usage matched E. coli expression; immune simulation predicted elevated IgG, IFN‑γ and IL‑2 responses.
analysis.contribution: The study provides a fully computationally evaluated mRNA vaccine candidate that may serve as a basis for experimental development against PUUV infection.
analysis.limitations: Results are limited to in silico analyses; experimental validation of translational efficiency, stability, immunogenicity and safety is required.

analysis.summary_en: Background: PUUV causes nephropathia epidemica, a zoonotic disease with renal complications and no approved vaccine. Methods: An immunoinformatics workflow designed an mRNA multi‑epitope vaccine (PV‑GNProtecta) using conserved G and N regions, with epitope prediction, population coverage, physicochemical profiling, structural validation, TLR4 docking, MD simulation, codon optimization, and immune simulation. Results: Identified epitopes were highly antigenic, non‑allergenic and non‑toxic; broad HLA coverage was predicted; the construct showed stability, solubility and antigenicity; 95.5% residues were in favored Ramachandran regions (ERRAT 91.4); docking/MM‑GBSA and a 100 ns MD indicated favorable TLR4 interaction; codon usage suited E. coli; immune simulation forecast increased IgG, IFN‑γ and IL‑2. Contribution: The data suggest PV‑GNProtecta as a promising candidate for further experimental vaccine development against PUUV. Limitations: Findings are purely computational; experimental validation is needed.

papers.title: Framing the 2026 Global Hantavirus Outbreak in Nigerian Online Newspapers: Insights from Premium Times and Sahara Reporters
papers.abstract: Background: Emerging infectious diseases often attract significant media attention because of their potential impact on public health perceptions and preparedness. Despite the absence of confirmed cases in Nigeria, the 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak generated global public health concern because of increased international mobility and the potential risk of cross-border transmission. Objective: This study investigated how Premium Times and Sahara Reporters framed the 2026 global hantavirus outbreak, focusing on the frequency, presentation formats, prominence, and dominant frames of coverage. Method: The study employed a content analysis design. Using census approach, all hantavirus-related stories published by Premium Times and Sahara Reporters between 2 and 30 May 2026 were identified, yielding 29 stories for analysis. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while Holsti’s (1969) formula was used to assess inter-coder reliability, yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.85. Results: Premium Times published 17 stories (58.6%), while Sahara Reporters published 12 stories (41.4%). Of the 29 stories, 24 (82.8%) were news stories, 19 (65.5%) received low prominence, and 10 (34.5%) adopted a health risk/awareness frame, followed by the prevention and safety measures frame (5 stories; 17.2%) and the attribution of responsibility frame (4 stories; 13.8%). Conclusion: Nigerian online newspapers reported the outbreak primarily as a public health risk but devoted limited attention and prominence to the issue, suggesting a predominantly reactive orientation in the newspapers' reporting of emerging health threats. Unique Contribution: This study contributes empirical evidence on Nigerian media framing of the 2026 global hantavirus outbreak and extends health communication scholarship on emerging zoonotic diseases. Key Recommendation: Nigerian online newspapers should adopt more sustained, prominent, explanatory, and interpretative reporting of emerging infectious diseases to strengthen public preparedness and risk communication.
authors: Valentine Okwudilichukwu Ezema, Sunday Uche Aja, Mercy Ifeyinwa Obichili, Joseph N. Chukwu, Chika Thonia Ezeali, Ijeoma Njideka Taiwo & Kelvin Chinemerem Nkwuda
papers.journal: International Journal of Sub-Saharan African Research

papers.title_zh: 在尼日利亚网络报纸中框定2026年全球 汉坦病毒 疫情:来自 Premium Times 与 Sahara Reporters 的洞见

analysis_zh.background: 新发传染病常因其对公众健康认知和防备的潜在影响而受到媒体的广泛关注 (A1);2026 年安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 疫情即使在尼日利亚未出现确诊病例,也引发了全球关注 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究采用内容分析设计 (A4);采用普查法,识别出 Premium Times 与 Sahara Reporters 在 2026 年 5 月 2 日至 30 日期间发布的所有与 汉坦病毒 相关的报道,共计 29 篇用于分析 (A5);数据使用描述性统计和 Holsti 公式进行分析,获得了 0.85 的编码员间信度系数 (A6)。
analysis_zh.results: Premium Times 发布了 17 篇报道 (58.6%),Sahara Reporters 发布了 12 篇报道 (41.4%) (A7);在 29 篇报道中,24 篇 (82.8%) 为新闻稿件,19 篇 (65.5%) 的版面突出度较低 (A8);最常见的框架是健康风险/意识 (34.5%),其次是预防与安全措施 (17.2%) 和责任归属 (13.8%) (A9)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提供了尼日利亚网络报纸对2026年全球 汉坦病毒 疫情框定的实证证据,拓展了新发人畜共患疾病健康传播研究的学术成果 (A11)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要,因而未在所提供的证据中报告详细的方法、更广的背景以及完整的结果。

papers.title: Human febrile illness associated with Yanggou tick virus: Clinical characteristics and epidemiological links to rodents.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: We identified Yanggou tick virus (YGTV), a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, in a patient presenting with fever and headache. This study aims to characterize the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of YGTV infection in patients with fever of unknown origin (FUO). METHODS: We conducted a surveillance study at the First Hospital of Jilin University (2020-2025) involving 1,011 patients with FUO. Concurrently, ticks and rodents in the vicinity of the patients' residences and workplaces were collected for viral detection. YGTV infection was confirmed via PCR assays. Positive samples were used for viral isolation, genome amplification, and phylogenetic characterization. An Apodemus agrarius challenge model was established to evaluate viral persistence and shedding. RESULTS: Of the 30 confirmed cases of YGTV infection, 10 were co-diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The patients showed no clear seasonality or geographic bias. Notably, rodent contact (43.3%) was a more frequent risk factor than tick bites (6.7%). While clinical presentations were non-specific, nearly 50% of the patients presented with gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. YGTV was isolated from patients, ticks, and A. agrarius (the latter often co-infected with Hantaan virus). Animal models confirmed persistent splenic infection and viral shedding via oral and fecal routes. CONCLUSION: Our findings establish YGTV as an underdiagnosed cause of human febrile illness, underscoring the transmission risks posed by tick vectors and rodent reservoirs. These results highlight the urgent need for enhanced clinical surveillance and diagnostic screening among patients presenting with FUO, particularly in regions where the virus is endemic.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Yanggou tick virus (YGTV), a segmented flavivirus, had not previously been recognized as a human pathogen. Methods: A surveillance study (2020‑2025) enrolled 1,011 FUO patients, collected ticks and rodents, confirmed YGTV by PCR, isolated and sequenced the virus, and used an Apodemus agrarius model to assess persistence and shedding. papers.title_zh: 与羊沟蜱病毒相关的人类发热疾病:临床特征及与啮齿动物的流行病学关联

analysis_zh.background: Yanggou蜱病毒(YGTV)是一种分段黄病毒,之前未被认定为人类致病病毒。
analysis_zh.methods: 一项监测研究(2020‐2025)在吉林大学第一医院纳入了1,011例不明原因发热患者;采集患者环境中的蜱和啮齿动物,采用PCR检测、分离、测序YGTV,并使用Apodemus agrarius挑战模型评估其持续感染和排泄情况。
analysis_zh.results: 确认了30例YGTV感染,其中10例合并诊断为肾综合征出血热;啮齿动物接触(43.3%)的报告频率高于蜱叮咬(6.7%);约一半患者出现胃肠或神经系统症状;病毒已从患者、蜱和A. agrarius中分离,动物实验显示脾脏持续感染并通过口腔和粪便排泄。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究确认YGTV是人类发热疾病的未被充分诊断的病因,并强调蜱和啮齿动物是传播风险的宿主,提示需加强临床监测和诊断筛查。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,限制了对研究设计、统计分析及更广泛流行病学背景的细节了解。

papers.title: Fractional optimal control of hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans
papers.abstract: This paper studies a fractional optimal control problem for a hantavirus transmission model involving interactions between rodent reservoirs and human populations. The model is formulated through a modified SIR–SIR structure, where both humans and rodents are divided into susceptible, infected, and recovered classes. The classical integer-order model is extended by using the Caputo fractional derivative, which captures memory and hereditary effects in the disease dynamics. Three time-dependent control variables are introduced: rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans. Positivity, boundedness, existence, and uniqueness of solutions are established to guarantee the biological and mathematical validity of the model. An optimal control problem is then formulated to minimize infected humans, infected rodents, and the costs of intervention. Necessary optimality conditions are derived using Pontryagin’s maximum principle for fractional systems. The adjoint equations, transversality conditions, and explicit characterization of the optimal controls are obtained. A numerical scheme based on the fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector method combined with the forward–backward sweep algorithm is implemented. Several numerical scenarios are investigated, including no control, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. The simulations show that the combined strategy gives the strongest reduction in both infected humans and infected rodents. The results illustrate how memory-dependent dynamics can alter the predicted transmission trajectories and optimal intervention profiles. However, empirical calibration and validation using compatible human and rodent surveillance data are required before the model can be used for outbreak-specific prediction.

Keywords Hantavirus transmission, Fractional optimal control, Caputo derivative, Pontryagin maximum principle, Fractional epidemic systems, Forward–backward sweep method Hantavirus infection is a serious zoonotic disease transmitted mainly through infected rodents and contaminated environmental materials such as urine, saliva, and feces1–3. The disease represents an important global public health challenge because of its high mortality rates, rapid respiratory complications, and increasing geographical spread4–6. Several strains of hantaviruses have been identified worldwide, including strains responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome7–9. Human infection generally occurs through inhalation of aerosolized particles from infected rodents, although evidence of human-to- human transmission has also been reported in specific outbreaks10 (Fig. 1). Rodents are considered the principal reservoirs of hantaviruses12,13. Long-term epidemiological studies confirmed that environmental conditions, climate fluctuations, rodent migration, and habitat changes play significant roles in the persistence and transmission of hantavirus infection14–18. In Asia and South America, several investigations revealed increasing prevalence rates associated with ecological changes and urbanization5,9,19. In Indonesia, hantavirus infections have attracted increasing scientific interest due to the existence of infected rodent reservoirs in several provinces20–22. Mathematical modeling has become an essential tool for understanding the spread and control of infectious diseases23–26. Classical epidemic models based on ordinary differential equations have been successfully applied to many zoonotic diseases27,28. Several mathematical models for hantavirus transmission have been developed in the literature. Abramson and Kenkre studied spatial and spatiotemporal patterns in hantavirus spread14,15. Allen et al. proposed deterministic and ecological models describing rodent-host interactions and environmental variability29–31. Wesley et al. analyzed direct and indirect transmission mechanisms in rodent Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:31685 2 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-72549-0 www.nature.com/scientificreports populations32. Additional modeling investigations involving ecological risk mapping, stochastic fluctuations, and environmental effects were developed in33–35. Although classical integer-order models provide useful qualitative insights, they often fail to capture memory and hereditary effects observed in biological systems. Many infectious diseases exhibit nonlocal temporal dynamics in which the future state depends not only on the present state but also on the history of the system. Fractional calculus provides a powerful mathematical framework for incorporating these memory effects into epidemiological models36–38. Fractional-order epidemic models have shown improved accuracy in describing long-memory biological processes and nonlinear transmission dynamics39. Biological justification for the Caputo derivative The use of the Caputo fractional derivative is motivated by biological and epidemiological processes that depend on accumulated history rather than only on the current state. Hantavirus risk is influenced by prior rodent abundance, repeated or prolonged contact with contaminated excreta, persistence of infectious material in the environment, delayed effects of habitat and climate variation, and time-distributed host recovery and immune responses. These mechanisms introduce temporal dependence that may not be represented adequately by a local first-order derivative. The Caputo operator describes such effects through a power-law memory kernel, so recent and earlier epidemic states contribute with different weights to the present rate of change. It is also suitable for population models because it permits conventional initial conditions expressed directly through the initial compartment sizes. The fractional order inline-eq-IEq1 is therefore interpreted as a phenomenological memory parameter. The value in l ine-eq-IEq2 recovers the memory-free classical model, whereas i n line-eq-IEq3 αne-eq-IEq3 represents nonlocal temporal dependence of increasing strength. Its epidemiological relevance should be assessed through sensitivity analysis, parameter estimation, and comparison with observed data. Recently, fractional optimal control theory has received considerable attention in mathematical biology and engineering40. The combination of fractional dynamics and optimal control allows the construction of realistic control strategies that account for memory-dependent disease behavior while minimizing intervention costs. Several important developments in fractional optimal control systems were established in41–43. Applications involving epidemic systems, cancer dynamics, and quantum systems, dark mater in cosmological models demonstrated the efficiency of fractional optimal control formulations44–48. Despite the large number of studies devoted to hantavirus transmission dynamics, very few works considered fractional-order optimal control formulations for hantavirus systems. Most existing models are formulated using classical differential equations without incorporating memory effects or optimal intervention strategies. Moreover, the combined effects of rodent reduction, environmental sanitation, and treatment controls within a fractional-order framework remain insufficiently investigated. Recent studies have demonstrated the value of combining fractional-order operators with biologically structured transmission mechanisms, parameter estimation, threshold analysis, and optimal control. Caputo fractional models have been developed for foot-and-mouth disease with environmental transmission and intervention strategies, as well as for norovirus transmission with vaccination and an environmental reservoir49,50. These studies illustrate how memory effects and environmental persistence can be incorporated into infectious- disease systems. Fractional rabies models have also provided several relevant methodological developments. Caputo models calibrated through Markov chain Monte Carlo methods have been used to estimate uncertain transmission parameters and evaluate public-health interventions51. Related investigations have considered dog vaccination within a Caputo framework52, and rabies dynamics formulated with the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative and MCMC parameter estimation53. Comparative analyses of singular and nonsingular fractional operators have further clarified how alternative memory kernels influence epidemic trajectories54. Moreover, fractional optimal control and cost-effectiveness analysis have been applied to rabies interventions, demonstrating the practical importance of combining memory-dependent dynamics with intervention design55. Several recent works have also strengthened the theoretical foundation of fractional epidemic modeling. In a related study, a fractional epidemiological model incorporating vaccination and quarantine compartments was analyzed with respect to well-posedness, threshold behavior, stability, and optimal intervention56. Motivated by these observations, this paper develops a new fractional optimal control model for hantavirus transmission dynamics between rodents and humans. The proposed model extends the classical hantavirus transmission framework by introducing Caputo fractional derivatives to capture hereditary effects in the disease dynamics. Three control variables are incorporated representing rodent elimination, environmental sanitation, and treatment efforts for infected individuals. Novelty of the study. The novelty of the present study lies in extending existing hantavirus transmission models in three connected directions. First, unlike classical integer-order models that describe rodent–human transmission without temporal memory, the proposed system uses the Caputo fractional derivative to represent hereditary and history-dependent effects. Second, the model integrates three intervention mechanisms— rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans—within a single optimal control framework. Third, the study provides a complete analytical and computational treatment, including positivity, boundedness, existence and uniqueness, equilibrium and stability analysis, the fractional Pontryagin optimality system, and a comparative assessment of no-control, single-control, and combined-control strategies. The main aim of this study is to develop and analyze a fractional optimal control model for hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans. The proposed model extends the classical SIR–SIR hantavirus framework by replacing the integer-order time derivative with the Caputo fractional derivative. This extension allows the model to account for memory effects, hereditary behavior, and the influence of past infection history on the current disease dynamics. The study also aims to design effective intervention strategies that reduce the number of infected humans and infected rodents while minimizing the cost of control implementation. To achieve this goal, three time- dependent controls are introduced: rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans. The mathematical analysis focuses on positivity, boundedness, existence, uniqueness, equilibrium behavior, and stability of the fractional model. In addition, Pontryagin’s maximum principle is used to derive the necessary optimality conditions, including the adjoint system and explicit control characterizations. A further aim is to investigate the numerical behavior of the model under different control scenarios and different fractional orders. The numerical simulations compare the uncontrolled case, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. The innovation of the work lies in combining fractional-order epidemic modeling, rodent– human transmission dynamics, and optimal control theory in one unified mathematical structure. Unlike classical integer-order models, the proposed system uses the Caputo fractional derivative to describe memory-dependent disease evolution. analysis.summary_en: Background: This paper studies hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans, a zoonotic disease with high mortality and expanding spread. Methods: A modified SIR–SIR model with Caputo fractional derivatives incorporates memory effects and three time‑dependent controls (rodent culling, sanitation, human treatment) and formulates an optimal control problem via Pontryagin’s maximum principle. Results: Numerical simulations using a fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector scheme show that combined control yields the greatest reduction in infected humans and rodents, illustrating altered transmission trajectories due to memory dependence. Contribution: The study extends hantavirus modeling by integrating fractional dynamics and optimal control, offering insights into how memory effects influence intervention strategies and highlighting potential for improved outbreak management. Limitations: The model lacks empirical calibration and validation with surveillance data, and no real‑world sample size or location is reported, limiting immediate applicability to specific outbreaks.

papers.title: Current State of Diagnostics of Hemorrhagic Fevers Caused by Viruses of the Genera Orthonairovirus, Phlebovirus, Orthohantavirus and Orthoflavivirus, Using the LAMP Method
papers.abstract: The work is an overview of the data on application of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the diagnosis of viral hemorrhagic fevers caused by pathogens belonging to the second pathogenicity group. The first part of the review provides a brief characterization of the main viral agents of hemorrhagic fevers from the families Nairoviridae, Phenuiviridae, Hantaviridae, and Flaviviridae. Special attention is given to the epidemiological significance of these pathogens and the challenges associated with their timely laboratory identification. The aim of the study was to analyze and systematize the data available in the literature sources on the use of LAMP as an alternative to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for diagnosing hemorrhagic fevers caused by these agents. The review considers the principal methods for registering LAMP results, including the turbidimetric method, immunochromatographic assays, the use of fluorescent dyes, metal-based indicators and pH-sensitive dyes. A comparative analysis of the analytical characteristics of existing LAMP reagent kits for each of the described agents is also presented. It is noted that there are currently no registered and widely available commercial LAMP reagent kits for detecting the genetic markers of these viruses. This underscores the need for further research, since the implementation of rapid and reliable diagnostic methods suitable for field use is a prerequisite for effective epidemic control measures. Therefore, the development of appropriate reagent kits based on the LAMP method represents a promising objective.

source_records.title: Current State of Diagnostics of Hemorrhagic Fevers Caused by Viruses of the Genera Orthonairovirus, Phlebovirus, Orthohantavirus and Orthoflavivirus, Using the LAMP Method
source_records.abstract: The work is an overview of the data on application of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the diagnosis of viral hemorrhagic fevers caused by pathogens belonging to the second pathogenicity group. The first part of the review provides a brief characterization of the main viral agents of hemorrhagic fevers from the families Nairoviridae, Phenuiviridae, Hantaviridae, and Flaviviridae. Special attention is given to the epidemiological significance of these pathogens and the challenges associated with their timely laboratory identification. The aim of the study was to analyze and systematize the data available in the literature sources on the use of LAMP as an alternative to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for diagnosing hemorrhagic fevers caused by these agents. The review considers the principal methods for registering LAMP results, including the turbidimetric method, immunochromatographic assays, the use of fluorescent dyes, metal-based indicators and pH-sensitive dyes. A comparative analysis of the analytical characteristics of existing LAMP reagent kits for each of the described agents is also presented. It is noted that there are currently no registered and widely available commercial LAMP reagent kits for detecting the genetic markers of these viruses. This underscores the need for further research, since the implementation of rapid and reliable diagnostic methods suitable for field use is a prerequisite for effective epidemic control measures. Therefore, the development of appropriate reagent kits based on the LAMP method represents a promising objective.

Чуб1 Современное состояние диагностики геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых вирусами родов Orthonairovirus, Phlebovirus, Orthohantavirus и Orthoflavivirus методом LAMP 1Государственный научный центр вирусологии и биотехнологии «Вектор», р.п. Кольцово, Российская Федерация; 2Новосибирский национальный исследовательский государственный университет, Новосибирск, Российская Федерация Представлен обзор данных о применении метода петлевой изотермической амплификации (loop mediated isothermal amplification, LAMP) для диагностики вирусных геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых возбудите­ лями, относящимися к II группе патогенности. Дана краткая характеристика основных вирусных возбудителей геморрагических лихорадок из семейств Nairoviridae, Phenuiviridae, Hantaviridae и Flaviviridae. Особое внимание уделено эпидемиологической значимости данных патогенов и сложности их своевременной лабораторной иден­ тификации. Основная цель работы заключалась в анализе и систематизации имеющихся в литературе данных об использовании метода LAMP как альтернативы ПЦР для диагностики геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых данными возбудителями. Рассмотрены основные методы детекции результатов LAMP, включая турбидиметри­ ческий метод, иммунохроматографический анализ, использование флуоресцентных красителей, металлоинди­ каторов и pH-чувствительных красителей. Проведен сравнительный анализ аналитических характеристик раз­ работанных наборов реагентов для LAMP-диагностики каждого из рассматриваемых возбудителей. Отмечается, что в настоящее время не существует зарегистрированных и широкодоступных коммерческих LAMP-наборов реагентов для выявления генетических маркеров данных вирусов. Это актуализирует необходимость дальнейших исследований, так как внедрение быстрых и надежных методов диагностики, пригодных для использования в полевых условиях, является необходимым условием эффективных противоэпидемических мероприятий. Таким образом, разработка соответствующих наборов реагентов на основе метода LAMP представляет собой перспек­ тивную задачу. Ключевые слова: геморрагическая лихорадка, изотермическая амплификация, LAMP, диагностика. Корреспондирующий автор: Беличенко Ксения Руслановна, e-mail: ksenbelichen@gmail.com. Такие серьезные заболевания часто вызывают вирусы I и II группы патогенности, со­ гласно российской классификации патогенных для человека микроорганизмов. К вирусам II группы патогенности, вызывающим ВГЛ у людей, относят­ ся некоторые представители родов Orthonairovirus (сем. Nairoviridae), Phlebovirus (сем. Phenuiviridae), Orthohantavirus (сем. Hantaviridae) и Orthoflavivirus (сем. Flaviviridae) (табл. 1). Эти вирусы, способные вызывать вспышки ВГЛ с высокой летальностью, представляют большой ин­ терес для здравоохранения. В роде Orthonairovirus CCHFV способен вы­ зывать Крымскую-Конго геморрагическую ли­ хорадку, переносимую клещами рода Hyalomma. Зарегистрированы случаи заболевания данной ли­ хорадкой в Азии, Юго-Западной и Юго-Восточной Европе и Африке [1]. Инфекция у человека может протекать как в легкой форме, без специфических клинических симптомов, так и в тяжелой форме, до­ стигая уровня летальности 40 % [2]. Геном CCHFV состоит из трех сегментов РНК с отрицательной по­ лярностью: S (1,7 кб), M (5,4 кб) и L (12,1 кб). Вирус обладает большим генетическим разнообразием и демонстрирует высокую изменчивость во всех трех сегментах. Так, разница в нуклеотидной последо­ вательности для S-сегмента составляет 20 %, для M – 31 %, для L – 22 % [3, 4]. В аминокислотной последовательности S- и L-сегменты также более консервативны (95 %), чем M-сегмент (до 75 %) [4]. Выделяется 7 генетических линий, основанных на S-сегменте: Африка 1–3, Азия 1, 2 и Европа 1, 2. RVFV из рода Phlebovirus является возбудите­ лем одноименного зоонозного заболевания, пере­ носимого комарами родов Aedes, Culex, Anopheles, Eretmapoites, Mansonia. Лихорадка долины Рифт была зарегистрирована в большинстве африканских стран, Саудовской Аравии и Йемене. Заболевание может протекать в тяжелой форме с ретинитом, ге­ патитом и энцефалитом, у 1 % пациентов развива­ ется геморрагическая лихорадка, уровень летально­ сти достигает 50 % [5, 6]. Геном вируса состоит из двух сегментов РНК с отрицательной полярностью M (3,9 кб) и L (6,4 кб) и одного сегмента амбисенс­ ной РНК – S (1,7 кб) [7]. Геном RVFV достаточно консервативен, лишь М-сегмент имеет небольшие различия в нуклеотидной (5 %) и аминокислотной (2 %) последовательности [8]. Хантавирусы (род Orthohantavirus) способны вызывать у человека геморрагическую лихорадку с почечным синдромом (ГЛПС) и хантавирусный пульмональный синдром (ХПС), передаваемые грызунами. Случаи заболевания ГЛПС, вызванные пре­имущественно вирусом Хантаан (HTNV), за­ регистрированы в Европе, России и Азии [9]. В за­ висимости от возбудителя уровень летальности до­ стигает 15 %.
